title: Beef and Stilton Pasty
subtitle: Beef chuck and Stilton in a crimped shortcrust with caramelised onions
excerpt: Beef and Stilton pasty is a rich, pub-style take on the classic crimped pastry parcel: braised beef chuck and crumbled Stilton with caramelised onions, sealed in shortcrust and baked. The Stilton melts into the filling as it bakes, giving it a sharp, creamy note that cuts through the richness of the beef.
sourceNotes: Stilton is one of the great British cheeses, produced in the East Midlands. Its combination with beef is a British pub pairing that appears in pies, burgers, and pasties. The cheese is always added after the filling cools , it melts during baking rather than cooking out.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked. Bake from frozen at 180°C fan for 55 to 60 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Braise the beef filling up to 3 days ahead. Cool completely before assembling.

content.text: Beef and Stilton pasty uses braised beef rather than raw beef in the filling, unlike a Cornish pasty which relies on the steam inside the pastry to cook the meat. The beef is braised ahead, cooled, and combined with Stilton and caramelised onions before filling the pastry. The Stilton must be added cold, after the filling has cooled, or it will dissolve completely into the meat.
Braise the beef and caramelise the onions

Season the beef. Brown in batches in a Dutch oven over high heat. Remove. Add {{unsalted-butter}} of butter to the same pot and cook {{onion}} sliced onions over low heat for 20 minutes until golden and caramelised.
Return the beef. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock and the thyme. Cover and braise at 160°C fan for 1.5 hours until the beef is completely tender. Remove the thyme. Cool the filling completely.
Fold {{stilton}} of crumbled Stilton into the cold filling. Taste and season: Stilton is salty, so the filling may not need much more.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Roll the pastry into 4 circles, about 25 cm across. Pile the filling onto one half of each circle. Brush the border with beaten egg. Fold, seal, and crimp. Cut a steam hole and brush with beaten egg. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until deeply golden.

items.symptom: The Stilton has completely melted and the filling is greasy
items.cause: The Stilton was added to a warm filling, so it pre-melted before baking.
items.fix: Make sure the filling is completely cold , refrigerator-cold , before folding in the Stilton. Cold cheese holds its shape longer in the oven.

items.symptom: The pastry base is soggy from the filling
items.cause: The braised beef filling was still wet when assembled.
items.fix: The filling should have reduced to a thick, almost dry mixture before cooling. Drain off any excess liquid before folding in the Stilton.

items.cause: Stilton is naturally very salty and the braised stock was also salted.
items.fix: Season the beef filling minimally, then taste after adding the Stilton before deciding whether to add any more.

items.symptom: The beef is still chewy inside the pasty
items.fix: Chuck steak for pasty filling should be braised until it falls apart when pressed , at least 1.5 hours. It will be reheated inside the pastry so it must be fully tender before assembly.

content.text: Beef and Stilton is a combination found across British pub menus in pies, burgers, and now pasties. Stilton's sharpness and creaminess make it a natural match for the umami of slowly braised beef, and the combination inside a crisp shortcrust is especially good. This is an elevated pub pasty: more complex than the traditional Cornish but clearly related to it in form.
